title: Αἰπόλος καὶ αἶγες ἄγριαι
titleEn: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats
part: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats (Chambry 17 · Perry 6)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 17 (= Perry 6). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Αἰπόλος τὰς αἶγας αὐτοῦ ἀπελάσας ἐπὶ νομήν, ὡς ἐθεάσατο ἀγρίαις αὐτὰς ἀναμιγείσας, ἑσπέρας ἐπιλαβούσης, πάσας εἰς τὸ ἑαυτοῦ σπήλαιον εἰσήλασε.
sentences.tr: Aipolos tas aigas autou apelasas epi nomēn, hōs etheasato agriais autas anamigeisas, hesperas epilabousēs, pasas eis to heautou spēlaion eisēlase.
sentences.l: A goatherd, having driven his goats off to pasture, when he saw them mingled with wild ones, evening having come on, drove them all into his own cave.
sentences.i: A goatherd had driven his goats out to pasture, and seeing that wild goats had mixed in among them, he drove the whole flock into his cave when evening came on.
sentences.n: ἑσπέρας ἐπιλαβούσης is a genitive absolute: a noun and a participle both in the genitive, standing outside the grammar of the main clause and supplying its circumstance — “evening having come on”. It is Greek's ordinary way of stacking background events, and this short fable leans on it five times over. ἀναμιγείσας is the aorist passive participle of ἀναμείγνυμι, “mixed in among”.

sentences.t: Τῇ δὲ ὑστεραίᾳ χειμῶνος πολλοῦ γενομένου, μὴ δυνάμενος ἐπὶ τὴν συνήθη νομὴν αὐτὰς παραγαγεῖν, ἔνδον ἐτημέλει, ταῖς μὲν ἰδίαις μετρίαν τροφὴν παραβάλλων πρὸς μόνον τὸ μὴ λιμώττειν, ταῖς δὲ ὀθνείαις πλείονα παρασωρεύων πρὸς τὸ καὶ αὐτὰς ἰδιοποιήσασθαι.
sentences.tr: Tēi de hysteraiāi cheimōnos pollou genomenou, mē dynamenos epi tēn synēthē nomēn autas paragagein, endon etēmelei, tais men idiais metrian trophēn paraballōn pros monon to mē limōttein, tais de othneiais pleiona parasōreuōn pros to kai autas idiopoiēsasthai.
sentences.l: And on the next day, a great storm having arisen, not being able to lead them out to the usual pasture, he tended them indoors, throwing to his own a moderate feed, only so that they should not go hungry, but heaping up more for the strangers, so as to make them too his own.
sentences.i: Next day a heavy storm blew up, and since he could not take them out to the usual pasture he tended them indoors — tossing his own goats just enough to keep them from going hungry, while heaping up more for the newcomers, so as to make them his as well.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute (χειμῶνος πολλοῦ γενομένου); χειμών is both “winter” and “storm”, here the weather that keeps a flock in. μέν… δέ… sets the two halves against each other — his own goats against the strangers — and is carried in English by the contrast alone, not by a word. πρὸς τό with the infinitive marks purpose, “with a view to…”; λιμώττω is “be hungry, go short”, not “starve”; ὀθνεῖος is “foreign, belonging to someone else”.

sentences.t: Παυσαμένου δὲ τοῦ χειμῶνος, ἐπειδὴ πάσας ἐπὶ νομὴν ἐξήγαγεν, αἱ ἄγριαι ἐπιλαβόμεναι τῶν ὀρῶν ἔφευγον.
sentences.tr: Pausamenou de tou cheimōnos, epeidē pasas epi nomēn exēgagen, hai agriai epilabomenai tōn orōn epheugon.
sentences.l: And the storm having ceased, when he led them all out to pasture, the wild ones, having taken to the mountains, were fleeing.
sentences.i: When the storm was over and he led them all out to pasture, the wild goats made for the hills and were gone.
sentences.n: ἐπιλαμβάνομαι with the genitive is “lay hold of, take to”. The imperfect ἔφευγον leaves the flight in progress rather than finished — they were away and running.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ ποιμένος ἀχαριστίαν αὐτῶν κατηγοροῦντος, εἴγε περιττοτέρας αὐταὶ τημελείας ἐπιτυχοῦσαι καταλείπουσιν αὐτόν, ἔφασαν ἐπιστραφεῖσαι· « Ἀλλὰ καὶ δι’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο μᾶλλον φυλαττόμεθα· εἰ γὰρ ἡμᾶς τὰς χθές σοι προσεληλυθυίας τῶν πάλαι σὺν σοὶ προετίμησας, δῆλον ὅτι, εἰ καὶ ἕτεραί σοι μετὰ ταῦτα προσπελάσουσιν, ἐκείνας ἡμῶν προκρινεῖς. »
sentences.tr: Tou de poimenos acharistian autōn katēgorountos, eige perittoteras autai tēmeleias epitychousai kataleipousin auton, ephasan epistrapheisai· « Alla kai di’ auto touto mallon phylattometha· ei gar hēmas tas chthes soi proselēlythyias tōn palai syn soi proetimēsas, dēlon hoti, ei kai heterai soi meta tauta prospelasousin, ekeinas hēmōn prokrineis. »
sentences.l: And the shepherd charging them with ingratitude — seeing that they, having met with more than ordinary care, were leaving him — they said, having turned round: « But for this very thing we are the more on our guard; for if you preferred us, the ones who came to you yesterday, over those long with you, it is plain that, if others too draw near you after this, you will choose them over us. »
sentences.i: The goatherd reproached them for ingratitude — that they were deserting him after receiving better care than the rest — and they turned and said, « That is the very reason we are on our guard. If you set us, who came to you only yesterday, above those who have been with you all along, then plainly, if others come to you later, you will prefer them to us. »
sentences.n: κατηγορέω takes the genitive of the person accused and the accusative of the charge. Greek freely makes an adverb attributive by putting the article in front of it: τὰς χθές σοι προσεληλυθυίας is “the ones-having-come-to-you yesterday”, τῶν πάλαι σὺν σοί “those long-since with you”. φυλαττόμεθα is middle, “we guard ourselves”. προκρινεῖς is future — the goats simply run the man's own habit forward.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ μὴ δεῖν τούτων ἀσμενίζεσθαι τὰς φιλίας οἳ τῶν παλαιῶν φίλων ἡμᾶς τοὺς προσφάτους προτιμῶσι, λογιζομένους ὅτι, κἂν ἡμῶν ἐγχρονιζόντων ἑτέροις φιλιάσωσιν, ἐκείνους προκρινοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi mē dein toutōn asmenizesthai tas philias hoi tōn palaiōn philōn hēmas tous prosphatous protimōsi, logizomenous hoti, kan hēmōn enchronizontōn heterois philiasōsin, ekeinous prokrinousin.
sentences.l: The story shows that one must not be glad of the friendships of those who prefer us, the recent ones, over their old friends, reckoning that, even if, we having grown long-standing, they make friends with others, they will prefer those.
sentences.i: The story shows that we should not welcome the friendship of men who set us, the newcomers, above their old friends — reflecting that once we are the old ones ourselves and they take up with others, they will prefer those to us.
sentences.n: The usual formula ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ here governs an infinitive (μὴ δεῖν) instead of the more common ὅτι-clause; the sense is unchanged. ἡμῶν ἐγχρονιζόντων is one more genitive absolute — “we having grown long-standing”, i.e. once we in turn are the old friends. κἄν is καὶ ἐάν run into one word by crasis, “even if”. In the goats' own speech the comparison carried a genitive (ἐκείνας ἡμῶν προκρινεῖς, “prefer them to us”); here προκρινοῦσιν stands alone and the “to us” is only implied. The moral otherwise repeats the goats' argument in the first person plural.
